newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary analysts see 10 bp H2 devaluation rate cut. [CORRECTED 14:25 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Hungary analysts see 10 bp H2 devaluation rate cut. [CORRECTED 14:25 GMT]

text.p: Hungary is likely to decide at the end of June to cut the monthly 1.1 (corrects figure from 1.2) percent devaluation rate by 10 basis points to further reduce inflation, analysts said on Tuesday.
"A July 1 cut seems to be certain," said Csaba Varga of Citibank.

The government and the National Bank of Hungary said earlier that before deciding on the devaluation rate, they would examine inflation and trade processes because making the cut prematurely could threaten the trade balance.

Analysts said that inflation, current account and consumption figures published recently were likely to enable the government to cut the devaluation rate slightly without risking a substantial widening of the trade gap.
"Both the current and the trade accounts seem to be going well," said Credit Suisse First Boston's Istvan Racz.
Torok Attila of Postabank Securities said the March current account figures published on Friday surprised most analysts.
"Many analysts expected a quicker growth of the deficits, but instead of that we saw surpluses."
The current account deficit fell by $19 million in March to $478 million, while the trade gap narrowed by $46 million to $393 million.
The analysts said that a 0.1 to 0.2 percentage point cut in the devaluation rate was possible from July 1, but the central bank was unlikely to introduce a larger cut than that.

"Caution is justified," Racz said, adding that Hungary will substantially reduce customs duties by the second half of the year, and household consumption was likely to increase later in the year as economic growth was seen picking up.
Hungary expects the gross domestic product (GDP) to grow by two to three percent this year compared with some one percent in 1996.
A rise in consumption would probably boost imports and this may harm the trade balance if the devaluation rate is cut too radically, analysts said.
They said a probable scenario was that the devaluation rate will be cut moderately on July 1, and later in the year another reduction would be made if the trade deficit remains at the planned levels.
A cut of around 0.1 percentage points would not affect the real effective exchange rate of the forint, but would have a substantial psychological effect. analysts said.
"We have had this 1.2 percent rate for quite a long time, and a cut means that inflation can go further down, at an even increasing pace," said Gabor Oblath of think-tank Kopint-Datorg.
Racz said that Hungary's inflation targets for 1998 were ambitious and this encouraged the government for a reduction in the devaluation rate.
Hungary plans to reduce year-on-year inflation to between 16 and 17 percent by December from 18.6 percent in April, and to between 13 and 14 percent by December 1998.
